controversies/when-is-the-millennium/que: When is the millennium: now, before Christ returns, or after?
controversies/when-is-the-millennium/sum: Revelation 20 mentions a thousand-year reign of Christ and the saints. Whether it is the present Church age (amillennialism), a future golden age before Christ returns (postmillennialism), or a literal kingdom after his return (premillennialism, historic or dispensational) has divided Christians since the second century, and continues to shape views of history, politics and mission.
controversies/when-is-the-millennium/sid: Revelation is a book of symbols and recapitulating visions. The thousand years is the whole time between Christ’s two comings, when Satan is bound so that the gospel reaches the nations and the saints reign with Christ. The rest of the New Testament knows one return, one resurrection and one judgement, and every historic church has confessed exactly that.
One clear coming, resurrection and judgement elsewhere in the New Testament (John 5:28–29; Matt 25:31–46)
Satan’s binding already announced by Jesus (Matt 12:29; Luke 10:18)
Consensus of Augustine, the medieval Church and the Reformers
Premillennialists: "came to life" must mean bodily resurrection both times in Rev 20:4–5
Satan seems anything but bound today

Christ already reigns with all authority, and he must reign until all enemies are under his feet. The gospel, like leaven, will permeate the world, and the Spirit will convert the nations before the end, producing a long era of peace and righteousness. That hope has historically fuelled revival, missions and reform.
Psalm 2 and 110: the nations as Christ’s inheritance
Predictions of apostasy before the end (2 Tim 3; Luke 18:8)
Twentieth-century catastrophes undermined confidence in progress

Read Revelation 19–20 as the narrative it is: Christ returns, the righteous are raised, and he reigns on a renewed earth before the final judgement. This was the faith of Papias, Justin and Irenaeus, who stood close to the apostles, and it honours the goodness of creation and the body.
Only one text mentions a millennium
Mixed population of glorified and mortal humans is unexplained

God’s promises mean what they say. He swore a land and a throne to Abraham’s and David’s descendants, and he will keep that oath to Israel in a literal thousand-year kingdom after rapturing the Church and judging the world in a seven-year tribulation. A consistent literal hermeneutic is the only safeguard against allegorising away God’s faithfulness.
Romans 11: a future for ethnic Israel
New Testament fulfils Israel’s hope in Christ and one people of God (Eph 2)
controversies/when-is-the-millennium/tim: Justin Martyr affirms a thousand-year reign in Jerusalem but admits many orthodox Christians disagree.
Irenaeus defends an earthly kingdom against Gnostics (Against Heresies 5).
Dionysius of Alexandria persuades Egyptian chiliasts led by Nepos to abandon literal millennialism.
Creed of Constantinople: Christ’s "kingdom shall have no end".
Augustine’s City of God 20 establishes the amillennial reading in the West.
Augsburg Confession XVII condemns "Jewish opinions" of an earthly millennium.
Great Awakening revivals feed Jonathan Edwards’ postmillennial hopes.
The Great Disappointment discredits Millerite date-setting.
The Scofield Reference Bible spreads dispensational premillennialism.
The Holy Office rules that mitigated millenarianism cannot safely be taught.
Clouse’s The Meaning of the Millennium: Four Views formalises the modern debate as a set of respectable options.
controversies/when-is-the-millennium/res: No ecumenical council has defined the millennium. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican and most Reformed churches are officially or practically amillennial; many evangelical and Pentecostal bodies require premillennialism, sometimes pretribulational. Within evangelicalism the question is usually treated as a secondary matter on which believers may differ.
controversies/when-is-the-millennium/con: Shaped how churches relate to politics: from Christendom (amillennial) and reform movements (postmillennial) to sectarian withdrawal or prophetic political activism (premillennial).
Produced denominational boundaries (e.g. statements of faith requiring premillennialism) and seminary identities.
Generated a huge popular prophecy culture in the 20th century.
controversies/will-there-be-a-rapture/qu: Will believers be "raptured" before a final tribulation?
controversies/will-there-be-a-rapture/su: Paul says believers alive at Christ’s coming will be "caught up ... to meet the Lord in the air" (1 Thess 4:17). Since the 1830s, premillennialists have debated whether this happens before (pretribulation), in the middle of (midtribulation), before the wrath within (pre-wrath), or after (posttribulation) a future seven-year tribulation, while most historic churches see it simply as part of Christ’s single, visible return.
controversies/will-there-be-a-rapture/si: Christ told us to watch for him, not for the Antichrist. Because the Church is not appointed to wrath, he will come for his bride before the tribulation and return with her afterwards. Only this preserves the imminence that the New Testament urges on every generation.
Church absent on earth in Rev 4–19
Matthew 24:29–31 places the gathering after the tribulation

Scripture repeatedly splits the final "week" at its midpoint. The Church will witness the Antichrist’s rise but will be taken at the last trumpet, before the great wrath of the final three and a half years.

Follow Jesus’ own order in Matthew 24: persecution by the Antichrist, cosmic signs, then the gathering of the elect, and only then the day of the Lord’s wrath. Believers face persecution but are spared God’s wrath.
Joel 2:31 places signs before the day of the Lord

There is one future coming of Christ. "Immediately after the tribulation of those days" he gathers his elect, and we rise to meet him and escort him to earth, as citizens went out to meet a king. The Church has always been called to endure, not escape, and this was the hope of Irenaeus and the early martyrs.

Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican churches read 1 Thessalonians 4 as describing the one glorious return of Christ at the end of history, when the dead are raised and the living transformed. Speculation about a seven-year tribulation and secret rapture is a 19th-century innovation built on a contested reading of Daniel 9.
Creeds confess one coming "to judge the living and the dead"
No early or medieval witness to a two-stage coming
Dispensationalists: Daniel’s seventieth week is still future
controversies/will-there-be-a-rapture/ti: Morgan Edwards, a Baptist in Pennsylvania, writes of saints caught up some time before the end (a debated precedent).
J. N. Darby and the Brethren develop the pretribulation rapture; contested claims connect it with Margaret Macdonald’s vision (1830).
Millerite failure turns many premillennialists away from date-setting towards futurism.
Niagara Bible Conference creed makes premillennialism a mark of the emerging fundamentalist network; pretribulationism wins out by c.1900 after internal debate.
Scofield Reference Bible teaches the pretribulation rapture.
George Ladd’s The Blessed Hope revives evangelical posttribulationism.
Hal Lindsey’s The Late Great Planet Earth becomes a bestseller, popularising the rapture worldwide.
Marvin Rosenthal launches the pre-wrath view.
The Left Behind novels (to 2007) sell tens of millions of copies.
controversies/will-there-be-a-rapture/re: Unresolved and largely confined to premillennial evangelical and Pentecostal circles. Many denominational statements (e.g. some Baptist and Pentecostal bodies) affirm pretribulationism; Ladd-style posttribulationism dominates evangelical academic premillennialism; the historic churches reject the two-stage framework altogether.
controversies/will-there-be-a-rapture/co: Created a distinctive popular eschatological culture (films, novels, prophecy conferences).
Influenced attitudes to politics, ecology and persecution: some critics charge escapism; posttribulationists stress readiness to suffer.
Periodic date-setting (1988, 2011 Harold Camping) has caused disillusionment.
controversies/may-christians-bear-the-sw: Pacifism, just war and the sword
From Tertullian to the peace churches and modern nuclear debates, Christians have disagreed whether followers of Jesus may kill in war, serve as soldiers or wield coercive office.

Jesus told us to love our enemies and told Peter to sheathe his sword. The cross is God’s way of defeating evil. For three centuries the Church’s teachers agreed that Christians do not kill. We may suffer for refusing, but we will not take the lives of those for whom Christ died.

Love seeks the neighbour’s good, including the neighbour being attacked. God gives rulers the sword to restrain evil. War is a terrible necessity in a fallen world, but it can be just if fought by legitimate authority, for a just cause, with right intention, as a last resort and with restraint toward the innocent.
Soldiers not told to leave the army

God ordains the sword for the world, but outside the perfection of Christ. Disciples belong to another kingdom; we neither fight nor rule by the sword, nor swear oaths, but live as a community of peace that shows the world what Christ’s rule looks like.
Origen: Christians fight for the emperor by prayer.
Constantine’s favour changes Christians’ relation to the army and state.
Augustine articulates principles of justified war.
The First Crusade sanctifies war as penitential pilgrimage.
Augsburg Confession XVI affirms just wars and condemns the Anabaptists.
Grotius’ On the Law of War and Peace.
US Catholic bishops’ The Challenge of Peace on nuclear deterrence.
Pope Francis’ Fratelli Tutti questions whether modern war can be just.

Unresolved. Just-war teaching is the official or majority position of Catholic, Orthodox (in practice), Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and most evangelical churches; the historic peace churches and growing numbers of Christians in other traditions hold to pacifism or principled nonviolence.
Shaped Christian participation in armies, states and international law.
Produced conscientious objection and peace churches.
Continues in debates over nuclear weapons, drones and humanitarian intervention.
